{{Short description|Loss of precision in numerical analysis}}
In [[numerical analysis]], '''catastrophic cancellation'''<ref name="handbook">{{cite book |last1=Muller |first1=Jean-Michel |last2=Brunie |first2=Nicolas |last3=de Dinechin |first3=Florent |last4=Jeannerod |first4=Claude-Pierre |last5=Joldes |first5=Mioara |last6=Lefèvre |first6=Vincent |last7=Melquiond |first7=Guillaume |last8=Revol |first8=Nathalie |author8-link=Nathalie Revol|last9=Torres |first9=Serge |title=Handbook of Floating-Point Arithmetic |date=2018 |publisher=Birkhäuser |location=Gewerbestrasse 11, 6330 Cham, Switzerland |isbn=978-3-319-76525-9 |page=102 |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-76526-6 |edition=2nd |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-76526-6}}</ref><ref name="goldberg">{{cite journal |last1=Goldberg |first1=David |title=What every computer scientist should know about floating-point arithmetic |journal=ACM Computing Surveys |date=March 1991 |volume=23 |issue=1 |pages=5–48 |doi=10.1145/103162.103163 |url=https://docs.oracle.com/cd/E19957-01/806-3568/ncg_goldberg.html |accessdate=2020-09-17 |publisher=Association for Computing Machinery |location=New York, NY, United States |s2cid=222008826 |issn=0360-0300}}</ref> is the phenomenon that subtracting good approximations to two nearby numbers may yield a very bad approximation to the difference of the original numbers.

For example, if there are two [[Wall stud|studs]], one <math>L_1 = 253.51\,\text{cm}</math> long and the other <math>L_2 = 252.49\,\text{cm}</math> long, and they are measured with a ruler that is good only to the centimeter, then the approximations could come out to be <math>\tilde L_1 = 254\,\text{cm}</math> and <math>\tilde L_2 = 252\,\text{cm}</math>.
These may be good approximations, in [[relative error]], to the true lengths: the approximations are in error by less than 0.2% of the true lengths, <math>|L_1 - \tilde L_1|/|L_1| < 0.2\%</math>.

However, if the ''approximate'' lengths are subtracted, the difference will be <math>\tilde L_1 - \tilde L_2 = 254\,\text{cm} - 252\,\text{cm} = 2\,\text{cm}</math>, even though the true difference between the lengths is <math>L_1 - L_2 = 253.51\,\text{cm} - 252.49\,\text{cm} = 1.02\,\text{cm}</math>.
The difference of the approximations, <math>2\,\text{cm}</math>, is in error by almost 100% of the magnitude of the difference of the 
true values, <math>1.02\,\text{cm}</math>.

Catastrophic cancellation is not affected by how large the inputs are&mdash;it applies just as much to large and small inputs.
It depends only on how large the ''difference'' is, and on the ''error'' of the inputs.
Exactly the same error would arise by subtracting <math>52\,\text{cm}</math> from <math>54\,\text{cm}</math> as approximations to <math>52.49\,\text{cm}</math> and <math>53.51\,\text{cm}</math>, or by subtracting <math>2.00052\,\text{km}</math> from <math>2.00054\,\text{km}</math> as approximations to <math>2.0005249\,\text{km}</math> and <math>2.0005351\,\text{km}</math>.

Catastrophic cancellation may happen even if the difference is computed exactly, as in the example above&mdash;it is not a property of any particular kind of arithmetic like [[floating-point arithmetic]]; rather, it is inherent to subtraction, when the ''inputs'' are approximations themselves.  Indeed, in floating-point arithmetic, when the inputs are close enough, the floating-point difference is computed exactly, by the [[Sterbenz lemma]]&mdash;there is no [[Round-off error|rounding error]] introduced by the floating-point subtraction operation.

== Formal analysis ==
Formally, catastrophic cancellation happens because subtraction is [[ill-conditioned]] at nearby inputs: even if approximations <math>\tilde x = x (1 + \delta_x)</math> and <math>\tilde y = y (1 + \delta_y)</math> have small [[relative error|relative errors]] <math>|\delta_x| = |x - \tilde x|/|x|</math> and <math>|\delta_y| = |y - \tilde y|/|y|</math> from true values <math>x</math> and <math>y</math>, respectively, the relative error of the difference <math>\tilde x - \tilde y</math> of the approximations from the difference <math>x - y</math> of the true values is inversely proportional to the difference of the true values:

<math display="block">
\begin{align}
  \tilde x - \tilde y
  &= x (1 + \delta_x) - y (1 + \delta_y)
   = x - y + x \delta_x - y \delta_y \\
  &= x - y + (x - y) \frac{x \delta_x - y \delta_y}{x - y} \\
  &= (x - y) \biggr(1 + \frac{x \delta_x - y \delta_y}{x - y}\biggr).
\end{align}
</math>

Thus, the relative error of the exact difference <math>\tilde x - \tilde y</math> of the approximations from the difference <math>x - y</math> of the true values is

<math display="block">
\left|\frac{x \delta_x - y \delta_y}{x - y}\right|.
</math>

which can be arbitrarily large if the true values <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> are close.

== In numerical algorithms ==
Subtracting nearby numbers in floating-point arithmetic does not always cause catastrophic cancellation, or even any error&mdash;by the [[Sterbenz lemma]], if the numbers are close enough the floating-point difference is exact.
But cancellation may ''amplify'' errors in the inputs that arose from rounding in other floating-point arithmetic.

=== Example: Difference of squares ===
Given numbers <math>x</math> and <math>y</math>, the naive attempt to compute the mathematical function
<math>x^2 - y^2</math>
by the floating-point arithmetic
<math>\operatorname{fl}(\operatorname{fl}(x^2) - \operatorname{fl}(y^2))</math>
is subject to catastrophic cancellation when <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> are close in magnitude, because the subtraction can expose the rounding errors in the squaring.
The alternative factoring
<math>(x + y) (x - y)</math>,
evaluated by the floating-point arithmetic
<math>\operatorname{fl}(\operatorname{fl}(x + y) \cdot \operatorname{fl}(x - y))</math>,
avoids catastrophic cancellation because it avoids introducing rounding error leading into the subtraction.<ref name="goldberg"/>

For example, if
<math>x = 1 + 2^{-29} \approx 1.0000000018626451</math>
and
<math>y = 1 + 2^{-30} \approx 1.0000000009313226</math>,
then the true value of the difference
<math>x^2 - y^2</math>
is
<math>2^{-29} \cdot (1 + 2^{-30} + 2^{-31}) \approx 1.8626451518330422 \times 10^{-9}</math>.
In [[Double-precision floating-point format|IEEE 754 binary64]] arithmetic, evaluating the alternative factoring
<math>(x + y) (x - y)</math>
gives the correct result exactly (with no rounding), but evaluating the naive expression
<math>x^2 - y^2</math>
gives the floating-point number
<math>2^{-29} = 1.8626451\underline{4923095703125} \times 10^{-9}</math>,
of which less than half the digits are correct and the other (underlined) digits reflect the missing terms <math>2^{-59} + 2^{-60}</math>, lost due to rounding when calculating the intermediate squared values.

=== Example: Complex arcsine ===
When computing the [[Inverse trigonometric functions#Extension to complex plane|complex arcsine]] function, one may be tempted to use the logarithmic formula directly:

<math display="block">
\arcsin(z) = i \log \bigl(\sqrt{1 - z^2} - i z\bigr).
</math>

However, suppose <math>z = i y</math> for <math>y \ll -1</math>.
Then <math>\sqrt{1 - z^2} \approx -y</math> and <math>i z = -y</math>; call the difference between them <math>\varepsilon</math>&mdash;a very small difference, nearly zero.
If <math>\sqrt{1 - z^2}</math> is evaluated in floating-point arithmetic giving

<math display="block">
\operatorname{fl}\Bigl(\sqrt{\operatorname{fl}(1 - \operatorname{fl}(z^2))}\Bigr)
= \sqrt{1 - z^2}(1 + \delta)
</math>

with any error <math>\delta \ne 0</math>, where <math>\operatorname{fl}(\cdots)</math> denotes floating-point rounding, then computing the difference

<math display="block">
\sqrt{1 - z^2}(1 + \delta) - i z
</math>

of two nearby numbers, both very close to <math>-y</math>, may amplify the error <math>\delta</math> in one input by a factor of <math>1/\varepsilon</math>&mdash;a very large factor because <math>\varepsilon</math> was nearly zero.
This may make the final error very large even if the error <math>\delta</math> in computing <math>\sqrt{1 - z^2}</math> is very small.

For instance, let <math>z = -1234567 i</math>.
The true value of <math>\arcsin(z)</math> is approximately <math>-14.71937803983977i</math>.
But using the naive logarithmic formula in [[Double-precision floating-point format|IEEE 754 binary64]] arithmetic&mdash;which computes <math>1 - z^2</math> exactly, and incurs only a single rounding error of <math>|\delta| < 2^{-53}</math> in <math>\sqrt{1 - z^2}</math>&mdash;may give the floating-point number nearest to <math>-14.719\underline{644263563968}i</math>, with only five out of sixteen digits correct and the remainder (underlined) all incorrect.

In the above case of <math>z = i y</math> for <math>y \ll -1</math>, using the identity <math>\arcsin(z) = -\arcsin(-z)</math> avoids cancellation because <math display=inline>\sqrt{1 - (-z)^2} = \sqrt{1 - z^2} \approx -y</math> but <math>i (-z) = -i z = y</math>, so the subtraction is effectively addition with the same sign which does not cancel.

=== Example: Radix conversion ===

Numerical constants in software programs are often written in decimal, such as in the C fragment <syntaxhighlight lang="C" inline>double x = 1.000000000000001;</syntaxhighlight> to declare and initialize an IEEE 754 binary64 variable named <code>x</code>.
However, <math>1.000000000000001</math> is not a binary64 floating-point number; the nearest one, which <code>x</code> will be initialized to in this fragment, is <math>1.0000000000000011102230246251565404236316680908203125 = 1 + 5\cdot 2^{-52}</math>.
Although the radix conversion from decimal floating-point to binary floating-point only incurs a small relative error, catastrophic cancellation may amplify it into a much larger one:

<syntaxhighlight lang="C">
double x = 1.000000000000001;  // rounded to 1 + 5*2^{-52}
double y = 1.000000000000002;  // rounded to 1 + 9*2^{-52}
double z = y - x;              // difference is exactly 4*2^{-52}
</syntaxhighlight>

The difference <math>1.000000000000002 - 1.000000000000001</math> is <math>0.000000000000001 = 1.0\times 10^{-15}</math>.
The relative errors of <code>x</code> from <math>1.000000000000001</math> and of <code>y</code> from <math>1.000000000000002</math> are both below <math>10^{-15} = 0.0000000000001\%</math>, and the floating-point subtraction <code>y - x</code> is computed exactly by the Sterbenz lemma.

But even though the inputs are good approximations, and even though the subtraction is computed exactly, the difference of the ''approximations'' <math>\tilde y - \tilde x = (1 + 9\cdot 2^{-52}) - (1 + 5\cdot 2^{-52}) = 4\cdot 2^{-52} \approx 8.88\times 10^{-16}</math> has a relative error of over <math>11\%</math> from the difference <math>1.0\times 10^{-15}</math> of the original values as written in decimal: catastrophic cancellation amplified a tiny error in radix conversion into a large error in the output.

=== Benign cancellation ===

Cancellation is sometimes useful and desirable in numerical algorithms.
For example, the [[2Sum|2Sum and Fast2Sum]] algorithms both rely on such cancellation after a rounding error in order to exactly compute what the error was in a floating-point addition operation as a floating-point number itself.

The function
<math>\log(1 + x)</math>,
if evaluated naively at points
<math>0 < x \lll 1</math>,
will lose most of the digits of <math>x</math> in rounding
<math>\operatorname{fl}(1 + x)</math>.
However, the function
<math>\log(1 + x)</math>
itself is [[well-conditioned]] at inputs near <math>0</math>.
Rewriting it as
<math display="block">
\log(1 + x) = x \frac{\log(1 + x)}{(1 + x) - 1}
</math>
exploits cancellation in
<math>\hat x := \operatorname{fl}(1 + x) - 1</math>
to avoid the error from
<math>\log(1 + x)</math>
evaluated directly.<ref name="goldberg"/>
This works because the cancellation in the numerator
<math>\log(\operatorname{fl}(1 + x)) = \hat x + O(\hat x^2)</math>
and the cancellation in the denominator
<math>\hat x = \operatorname{fl}(1 + x) - 1</math>
counteract each other; the function
<math>\mu(\xi) = \log(1 + \xi)/\xi</math>
is well-enough conditioned near zero that
<math>\mu(\hat x)</math>
gives a good approximation to
<math>\mu(x)</math>,
and thus
<math>x\cdot \mu(\hat x)</math>
gives a good approximation to
<math>x\cdot \mu(x) = \log(1 + x)</math>.
